content: Aspiration pneumonitis is a clinical condition caused by the inhalation of gastric contents into the lungs. Its incidence in obstetric anesthesia has significantly decreased due to advancements in anesthetic techniques and the widespread adoption of regional anesthesia during cesarean sections. However, aspiration pneumonitis remains a notable cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, necessitating effective preventive measures. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether specific interventions administered prior to cesarean sections can reduce the risk of aspiration pneumonitis in women with uncomplicated pregnancies. The review included randomized controlled trials, while quasi-randomized trials were excluded. A systematic search was conducted, and data from eligible studies were independently assessed for inclusion, bias risk, and extracted for analysis. Fixed-effect meta-analysis was employed when studies were deemed to estimate the same treatment effect, while random-effects analysis was used in cases of significant clinical or statistical heterogeneity. A total of 32 studies were included in the review, but only 22 studies involving 2,658 women provided data for analysis. All participants underwent cesarean sections under general anesthesia. The studies examined various interventions, but most were small in scale and of unclear or poor methodological quality. When compared to no treatment or placebo, the use of antacids significantly reduced the risk of intragastric pH falling below 2.5 (risk ratio [RR] 0.17, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.09 to 0.32; two studies, 108 women). Similarly, H2 receptor antagonists demonstrated a significant reduction in this risk (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.18; two studies, 170 women), as did proton pump inhibitors (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.46; one study, 80 women). When comparing H2 receptor antagonists to proton pump inhibitors, H2 receptor antagonists were associated with a lower risk of intragastric pH < 2.5 at the time of intubation (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.97; one study, 120 women). However, the comparison between H2 receptor antagonists and antacids yielded unclear results. The combination of antacids and H2 receptor antagonists was significantly more effective in reducing the risk of intragastric pH < 2.5 at intubation compared to placebo (RR 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.15; one study, 89 women) and compared to antacids alone (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.92; one study, 119 women). The authors concluded that while the overall quality of evidence was poor, the findings suggest that the combination of antacids and H2 receptor antagonists is more effective than no intervention and superior to antacids alone in preventing low gastric pH. However, none of the included studies evaluated potential adverse effects or clinically significant outcomes. These findings are applicable to all women undergoing cesarean sections under general anesthesia.
